A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, algorithms, objectives and central theoretical results. Their complete text, equations, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports theoretical bounds, constructions and proofs, including its appendices. It contains no original experimental or simulation outcomes; empirical studies mentioned are attributed to other work.

after.justification: v3 Section 4 and Figures 1–3 report original two-armed bandit simulations, linear-bandit simulations and MNIST experiments. Appendix C supplies experimental details.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–4 retain their reward estimation, pessimistic correction where applicable, and policy construction procedures. Practical estimation suggestions and new experimental feature representations do not establish a revision to the proposed algorithms.

E1.justification: v2 has no empirical evaluation coverage. v3 adds two-armed bandit simulations, synthetic linear bandits and a contextual-bandit evaluation using MNIST images as contexts and digit labels as actions.

E2.justification: Neither version reports empirical comparisons against baseline algorithms. The new experiments vary reference policies and regularizers for the proposed methods. Table 1 retains the same analytical comparisons with Xiong et al. (2024) and Zhao et al. (2024).

E3.justification: v3 introduces sample-size sweeps, regularized suboptimality measurements, log-log rate fitting, controlled reference-policy mixtures and an alpha-scaling experiment. These are new evaluation protocols. The alpha experiment has an unresolved setting discrepancy: Section 4 states nα = 2^15, while Figure 1 labels nα = 2^18.

E4.justification: v3 adds sensitivity analyses absent from v2: changing behavior-policy coverage across all three testbeds and varying the strong-convexity modulus jointly with sample size. These examine whether KL and chi-squared regularization exhibit the predicted differences in coverage dependence and alpha scaling.

E5.justification: Figure 1 newly specifies averages over 100 independent trials and estimates convergence slopes using linear regression. No comparable empirical statistical reporting exists in v2. v3 does not provide confidence intervals or clearly extend the stated trial count to Figures 2–3.

E6.justification: v3 adds the first empirical results. Figure 1 reports fitted slopes of -0.98 and -0.97 for KL, and -0.98 and -0.99 for chi-squared regularization. Figures 2–3 add coverage-dependent suboptimality curves for linear bandits and MNIST. These are newly reported outcomes, not same-setting improvements over v2.

T1.justification: New Propositions B.1–B.2 construct contrasting relationships between the two coverage measures. The dueling-bandit upper bound changes from a D²_{π*} factor in v2 Theorem D.1 to min(D²_{π*}, C_{π*}) in v3 Theorem F.4; its lower-bound statement also changes coverage measures. Additional revisions include Theorem 3.4's conditions and proof perturbation, weaker moment-lemma assumptions, and explicit expectations in the auxiliary lower-bound lemmas. Most existing proofs otherwise remain or relocate.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list newly claim numerical verification of the theoretical rates. The central claims concerning fast rates, single-policy coverage for KL, coverage independence for strongly convex f, and extension to dueling bandits remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 adds an explanation of why easy instances can outperform a worst-case lower bound without contradiction (Remark 2.13), and interprets the new experimental coverage and alpha trends. The conclusion makes the remaining D²-versus-C gap explicit; the smoothness and strong-convexity limitations were already present in v2.

D1.justification: New Appendix C documents the 20-dimensional, 100-arm simulation, normalized feature and parameter construction, and MNIST embeddings expanded from 10 to 100 dimensions. Remark 2.6 additionally describes practical D² estimation using visitation frequencies, empirical covariance and heuristics. These add substantial implementation information, although classifier training details and code access remain unspecified.

R1.justification: v3 adds Aminian et al. (2025), expands connections to counterfactual risk minimization and offline policy learning, and credits Abernethy et al. (2015) for the dual-Bregman perspective. Additional citations support practical estimation and experiments. The main positioning against prior KL analyses remains; Di and Huang publication updates are not new works.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract and contribution narrative, turns Section 2.4 into a proof overview, and moves its detailed argument to Appendix D. The former dueling-bandit section moves into Appendix F, experiments occupy Section 4, and references precede a new contents listing and reorganized appendices.

P2.justification: v3 adds three multipanel experimental figures containing seven plots. It also adopts ICLR typography and headers and compacts algorithm displays, including removal of the duplicated least-squares expression in Algorithm 1. Table 1 retains its substantive entries.

improvement.justification: v3 adds useful empirical checks, clearer explanations and a revised lower-bound proof. However, its newly strengthened Theorem F.4 claims min(D²_{π*}, C_{π*}) dependence while Appendix G.1, Equation G.10, still concludes only the D²-dependent bound. The alpha-scaling setup also conflicts with Figure 1's legend. These additions improve support but introduce unresolved issues in a stated guarantee and experimental documentation, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
